questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the producers that form the base of a food web
questions.stem: A civil engineer sizing the primary-production module of a recirculating wetland asks which organisms form the base of its food web.

options.text: Nitrifying bacteria that oxidise ammonia into nutrients that rooted plants then absorb
options.misconception: treats nitrogen-cycling bacteria as the producer base

options.text: Green algae and submerged plants that fix solar energy into biomass by photosynthesis
Filter-feeding mussels that strain plankton and other suspended food from the water
options.misconception: mistakes a plankton consumer for the base of the food web

options.text: Burrowing beetles that fragment and bury dead plant matter in the sediment layer
options.misconception: treats a detritivore working on dead matter as a producer

questions.explanation: Producers fix solar energy into plant and algal biomass, and every consumer depends on it. Bacteria, mussels and beetles gain energy by consuming material, so none is the base.
questions.hint: Ask which organisms build their own food from sunlight.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate energy transferred to the next trophic level
questions.stem: A process engineer measures 1,000 kJ of energy entering a grassland food web as plant biomass in one year. How many kJ reach primary consumers?
questions.explanation: About ten percent of producer energy passes to herbivores, so 1,000 kJ of plant biomass supports about 100 kJ at the primary consumer level. The rest is used in metabolism and released as heat.
questions.hint: Apply the ten percent transfer rule to the producer total.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate claims that ignore trophic transfer efficiency
questions.stem: A landscape contractor claims that tripling the grass in a field will triple the rabbit population, and asks you to judge the reasoning.

options.text: Tripling the grass triples the rabbits, because rabbit numbers track grass volume directly
options.misconception: assumes consumer numbers scale with producer biomass

options.text: Rabbit numbers stay the same, because grass volume never limits a population in open field
options.misconception: denies that producer biomass can limit consumer numbers

options.text: Rabbit numbers will rise, but far less than threefold, because transfer efficiency caps the energy they get
Rabbits triple only if the grass is fertilised with nitrogen at the start of the season
options.misconception: confuses one nutrient with the real transfer ceiling

questions.explanation: Because only about a tenth of plant energy reaches herbivores, extra grass adds far less energy than it adds biomass. Rabbits may increase, but not threefold, so the contractor's linear scaling fails.
questions.hint: Think about energy lost between the two levels.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an energy budget across trophic levels
questions.stem: A sensor engineer logs joules per day in a fish pond: 40,000 J fixed by algae, 4,000 J in copepods and 400 J in small fish. What does this pattern show?

options.text: Most captured energy leaves as heat through respiration instead of passing to the next level
The pond gains energy overall, because fixed sunlight exceeds the energy held in the fish
options.misconception: treats captured energy as newly created energy in the pond

options.text: The copepods and fish are failing to thrive, since such steep drops signal poor health
options.misconception: reads normal energy loss as evidence of illness

options.text: The measurements must be faulty, because energy cannot fall between trophic levels
options.misconception: believes energy must persist as biomass at every level

questions.explanation: Only a fraction of energy passes to the next level; the rest is used in metabolism and released as heat. The tenfold drop from algae to copepods to fish is the expected signature of that loss.
questions.hint: Energy is conserved overall, but not retained as biomass.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the expected shape of a biomass pyramid
questions.stem: A utility planner compares the biomass standing in a lake at four feeding levels and wants to know which pyramid shape is expected.

options.text: An upright biomass pyramid, because producers usually outweigh the consumers feeding on them
A flat biomass pyramid, because biomass stays equal at each feeding level in a stable lake
options.misconception: believes equal productivity forces equal standing biomass

options.text: A spindle-shaped pyramid, because the middle levels are always the largest part of a lake
options.misconception: confuses a rare mid-level bloom with the normal shape

options.text: An inverted biomass pyramid, because phytoplankton always outweigh the fish that graze them
options.misconception: assumes the inverted shape occurs in every aquatic system

questions.explanation: Most systems have producers holding the most biomass, with each level holding less. An inverted pyramid is exceptional, seen where fast-turning phytoplankton support a heavier consumer stock.
questions.hint: Consider which level usually holds the most living material.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute energy dissipated by decomposers processing detritus
questions.stem: A compost engineer sends 40,000 kJ of dead plant material into a hot heap where decomposers convert 10 percent of it into their own biomass. How many kJ are dissipated as heat?
questions.explanation: Decomposers keep only a tenth of the detritus energy as new biomass, which is 4,000 kJ, so the remaining 36,000 kJ is respired and lost as heat. The heap heat output measures that loss.
questions.hint: Subtract the fraction converted into biomass from the total.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a mixed diet links several trophic levels
questions.stem: An agronomist notes that the estate's foxes eat rabbits, berries and grain, and asks what this feeding pattern implies.

options.text: Foxes are pure carnivores with a flexible diet that still counts as one fixed level
options.misconception: treats a flexible diet as a single fixed trophic position

options.text: Foxes compete directly with grain-eating birds, because both take energy from plants
options.misconception: assumes omnivores only ever compete with other plant eaters

options.text: Foxes gain energy from several trophic levels, so they can move energy between those levels
Foxes must sit above grain in the food web, since berries are only a minor supplement
options.misconception: assumes a dominant diet determines a species' trophic level

questions.explanation: An omnivore draws energy from more than one trophic level, so it links them and can transfer energy from a lower level to a higher one. Its position in the web is therefore flexible.
questions.hint: Consider what a mixed diet does to energy transfer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise exponential growth from a series of population counts
questions.stem: A hatchery technician counts bacterial colonies of 100, 150, 225 and 340 on successive days of a culture. Which growth pattern fits best?

options.text: Logistic, since the daily gains are shrinking and the culture must be at carrying capacity
options.misconception: claims slowing growth proves capacity has been reached

options.text: Exponential, since the percentage increase stays near 50 percent each day
Stationary, since the colony count barely changes between the first and last reading
options.misconception: ignores the large percentage increase in later readings

options.text: Seasonal, since the count follows a smooth yearly cycle of growth and decline
options.misconception: reads four days of data as a full seasonal cycle

questions.explanation: Each day's gain is a roughly constant fraction of the previous count, which is the signature of exponential growth. Logistic growth would show a declining percentage increase.
questions.hint: Compare each increase with the count that preceded it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the response of a population overshooting its carrying capacity
questions.stem: A ranch manager asks what would happen to a sheep flock that is allowed to expand well past its pasture's carrying capacity.

options.text: Numbers keep rising slowly, because density-dependent limits only slow growth a little
options.misconception: underestimates how sharply overcrowding crashes a population

options.text: Numbers stay level, because the flock cannot reproduce while the pasture is full
options.misconception: assumes reproduction stops before capacity is exceeded

options.text: Numbers rise, then plateau, because sheep adjust perfectly to every resource shortage
options.misconception: assumes animals can adjust away a severe resource shortage

options.text: Numbers rise first, then fall sharply as resources run out and the land is overgrazed

questions.explanation: Pasture, water and space set a carrying capacity, and pushing a flock past it causes starvation and disease, so the population crashes. A plateau occurs near the limit, not beyond it.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when demand exceeds the supply.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Apply a density-dependent mortality rate to a population count
questions.stem: A wildlife engineer notes that 640 voles trigger density-dependent mortality that removes 15 percent of individuals whenever the count passes 500. How many voles remain?
questions.explanation: The cull removes 15 percent of 640, which is 96 animals, leaving 640 minus 96, or 544 voles. The result still sits above the 500 threshold, so the density-dependent process would keep acting.
questions.hint: Take fifteen percent off the initial count.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Spot why a green space still needs a producer base
questions.stem: A landscaping crew is told the new plaza will be self-sustaining because it will contain both plants and insects. What is the flaw?

options.text: Insects pollinate the plants, so the plaza can produce its own food indefinitely
options.misconception: confuses pollination services with energy capture

options.text: The plaza needs no soil, because insects aerate and enrich the ground for the plants
options.misconception: believes soil fertility comes from animals not decay

options.text: The plaza is fine, because plants and insects together form a complete food web
options.misconception: treats a two-part system as a complete food web

options.text: Insects are consumers, so a green space still depends on plants for the energy it needs

questions.explanation: A food web needs a producer base, and insects obtain energy by eating rather than capturing sunlight. Without plants, or another producer, the insects in the plaza would quickly run out of energy.
questions.hint: Check which group actually captures solar energy.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret rising standing crop as evidence of primary productivity
questions.stem: A plant ecologist measures the same grass field for three summers and logs standing crop of 800, 950 and 1,200 grams per square metre. What does the trend suggest?

options.text: Rising primary productivity, which should eventually support more herbivores in the field
A growing population of grass itself, which explains the rising standing crop each summer
options.misconception: mistakes rising plant biomass for a rising plant population

options.text: Rising decomposer activity, since more dead material returns nutrients to the soil each year
options.misconception: reads plant growth as evidence of faster decomposition

options.text: A growing herbivore population, which is grazing less each year and leaving more grass
options.misconception: infers grazer decline without any grazing data

questions.explanation: More standing crop per square metre indicates higher primary productivity in that field, which is the energy base for herbivores. The trend says nothing about plant numbers or grazers.
questions.hint: Standing crop is a measure of captured producer energy.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the ten percent rule correctly and reject similar-sounding claims
questions.stem: A marine engineer explains why a food chain supports few large fish and asks which reasoning captures the rule.

options.text: Each level contains fewer organisms, so the top level holds the least energy
options.misconception: confuses number of organisms with energy at each level

options.text: Each level keeps only a fraction of the energy, so the top level holds the least energy
Each level loses biomass to waste, so the top level holds the least energy
options.misconception: treats the rule as a statement about biomass only

options.text: Each level is colder, so the top level holds the least energy
options.misconception: invents a temperature effect to explain the energy pattern

questions.explanation: The rule of ten percent is about energy transfer, not organism numbers or discarded biomass. Because only a fraction of the energy at each level is passed on, the highest level holds least.
questions.hint: Focus on energy, not on how many animals there are.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute the energy reaching the top of a four-level pyramid
questions.stem: A grassland pyramid carries 10,000 kJ at the producer level, 1,000 kJ at the primary consumer level, 100 kJ at the secondary level and 10 kJ at the tertiary level. How much energy reaches the tertiary level in kilojoules?
questions.explanation: Each step in the pyramid passes on a tenth of the energy below it, so 10,000 becomes 1,000, then 100, then 10 kJ. The tertiary level therefore holds 10 kJ, a thousandth of the producer total.
questions.hint: Apply the ten percent rule at each of the three steps.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why energy and biomass pyramids can differ
questions.stem: A fisheries analyst says an energy pyramid and a biomass pyramid can look different in the same lake. Why is that possible?

options.text: Fast turnover can make a small standing biomass of producers support a larger consumer biomass
Biomass pyramids measure numbers of organisms while energy pyramids measure their mass
options.misconception: switches the definitions of biomass and energy

options.text: The two pyramids must match, so any difference means one measurement was done wrong
options.misconception: denies that energy and biomass can genuinely differ

options.text: Energy pyramids are always upright, but biomass pyramids change shape with the season
options.misconception: assumes energy pyramids can invert like biomass pyramids

questions.explanation: An energy pyramid always narrows upward because energy is lost at each step, but standing biomass depends on turnover. Phytoplankton can hold a small crop yet support heavier consumers.
questions.hint: Think about how fast a population is renewed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret mass loss from a decomposing litter bag
questions.stem: A soil scientist weighs a leaf-litter bag before and after six months of decomposition and finds it has lost 80 percent of its mass. What happened to most of that mass?

options.text: Most of it was washed away as dissolved ions that the soil retained for plant roots
options.misconception: assumes litter mass mostly becomes dissolved plant nutrients

options.text: Most of it was converted into new organic matter that is now part of the soil humus
options.misconception: confuses total loss with loss of decomposer respiration

options.text: Most of it was metabolised by detritivores and fungi and released as carbon dioxide and heat
Most of it was eaten by earthworms and passed on as worm biomass in the soil
options.misconception: assumes a single detritivore group removed all the mass

questions.explanation: Decomposition releases most of the energy in dead material as heat through respiration, so litter mass falls quickly. Only a fraction becomes detritivore biomass, dissolved nutrients or new humus.
questions.hint: Ask where the carbon in decomposing leaves ends up.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how omnivory spreads predation pressure across prey types
questions.stem: A pest control officer explains why the estate's foxes keep the vole numbers down without collapsing the hare population.

options.text: Foxes hunt hares only, and hares naturally outnumber and outlast the voles
options.misconception: claims foxes ignore the smaller prey that dominates

options.text: Foxes are too scarce to affect vole numbers, which are controlled only by grass cover
options.misconception: denies that predators can shape small-prey populations

options.text: Foxes eat grass as well, so they are really competitors of the grazing hares
options.misconception: assumes foxes compete with hares for vegetation

options.text: Foxes switch between prey types, so they restrain voles while still eating hares

questions.explanation: An omnivore spreads its predation across several prey types, so it can hold down one small rodent while still taking some hares. This flexible pressure restrains the rodents.
questions.hint: Consider what a mixed diet does to predation pressure.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a compounded population increase over two time steps
questions.stem: A culture starts with 250 cells growing at 20 percent per hour. If the rate holds, how many cells are present after two hours?
questions.explanation: Compounding at 20 percent per hour gives 250 times 1.2 squared, which is 360 cells. Exponential growth multiplies rather than adds, so the hourly gains themselves grow over time.
questions.hint: Multiply by 1.2 once for each hour.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about why a reduced population does not simply regrow
questions.stem: A game reserve manager argues that reducing the deer herd to half will double the grass available for the herd.

options.text: Doubling the grass per animal will double the herd once the extra grass is fully exploited
options.misconception: assumes unlimited exploitation of extra forage

options.text: Halving the herd will halve the grass, because grass supply depends on herbivore density
options.misconception: assumes grass production falls when herbivores decline

options.text: The herd size is set by social behaviour alone, so forage changes make no difference at all
options.misconception: denies that food supply limits herd size at all

options.text: Doubling the grass per animal does not double the herd, because the herd is limited by more than grass

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity reflects every limiting factor, not just grass. Lowering the herd raises per-animal forage, but the herd will not double back to the old limit, because other limits apply.
questions.hint: Think about what else limits a herd besides forage.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify density-dependent limits from a slowing growth rate
questions.stem: A field team counts 200, 380, 700, 1,150 and 1,600 plants in five plots of equal area as the growing season progresses. What limits the final count?

options.text: Density-independent limits, because the count stopped rising during a week of heavy rain
options.misconception: reads a slowing trend as proof of a weather-driven limit

options.text: No limit is operating, since the population is still growing at the end of the season
options.misconception: ignores the clear drop in the rate of increase

options.text: Density-dependent limits, because the rate of increase slows as crowding and competition increase
Emigration alone, because the number of seeds in the plots stayed constant all season
options.misconception: assumes seed supply explains a drop in growth rate

questions.explanation: The gains between counts shrink each time even though the population keeps rising, which is the pattern of density-dependent limits such as competition and disease. Weather events cause abrupt dips.
questions.hint: Look at how the interval gains change over time.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Select the planting that rebuilds a food web from its base
questions.stem: A mangrove restoration crew is told which planting will rebuild the food web fastest, and the answer depends on the base.

options.text: Crabs, because their burrowing aerates the mud and keeps the seedlings rooted
options.misconception: mistakes a mud-burrowing consumer for a producer

options.text: Herons, because they control the fish that would otherwise eat the seedlings
options.misconception: treats a predator of fish as a producer of the system

options.text: Barnacles on the stems, because they filter plankton and enrich the water
options.misconception: treats a plankton filter feeder as the producer base

options.text: Mangrove trees, because their leaf litter and roots feed the whole web from below

questions.explanation: Mangroves are the producers of the system, and their litter and detritus feed the invertebrates and fish that support everything above them. Crabs, herons and barnacles are all consumers in that web.
questions.hint: Identify the organism that makes its own food.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate energy available to a top consumer level
questions.stem: A reservoir engineer estimates that the plankton biomass in a lake holds 500,000 kJ of energy. How much energy is available to tertiary consumers in that lake?
questions.explanation: Energy passes to the next level at about a tenth, so 500,000 kJ supports 50,000 kJ at the primary consumer level, 5,000 kJ at the secondary level and 500 kJ at the tertiary level.
questions.hint: Step down three levels at ten percent each.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Critique claims that link feed quality directly to population triples
questions.stem: A fish feed designer claims a pellet with 40 percent protein will support twice the fish as one with 20 percent. What is the flaw?

options.text: Protein is the only limit on growth, so doubling it really does double the population
options.misconception: treats a single nutrient as the whole limiting system

options.text: Doubling the protein in the feed does not double the fish, because transfer efficiency caps growth
Doubling protein halves oxygen demand, so the system can hold twice as many fish
options.misconception: invents an oxygen benefit that is not measured

options.text: The claim holds only if the water temperature also rises by the same proportion
options.misconception: makes growth depend on a proportional temperature change

questions.explanation: Energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient, so extra protein in a diet is only partly converted into new fish tissue. Raising feed quality helps, but far short of a doubling.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to energy that is not converted.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a temperature series from a composting heap
questions.stem: A compost engineer records pile temperatures of 20, 45, 60 and 38 degrees over four days of a heap. Which statement best fits these readings?

options.text: Sunlight is heating the pile more strongly as the day progresses each time
options.misconception: attributes microbial heat to solar heating of the heap

options.text: The pile is cooling because the decomposers have finished all the available material
options.misconception: reads a cooling trend as the end of decomposition

options.text: Microbial respiration is releasing heat as decomposers work through the organic material
Insulation is failing, since a working heap should hold a perfectly steady temperature
options.misconception: assumes decomposition gives a constant temperature

questions.explanation: The temperature peak shows active microbial respiration releasing energy as heat, followed by a decline as easily digested material is used up. A steady or rising profile points to another cause.
questions.hint: Heat in a compost pile comes from respiration.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Relate turbidity and turnover to biomass pyramid shape
questions.stem: A water-quality team compares pyramids for a clear lake and a turbid one and asks why their shapes can differ.

options.text: Clear water always produces the widest pyramid because light reaches the bottom
options.misconception: assumes clearer water always means a broader energy base

options.text: Turbid water lets small, fast-turning producers support more consumer biomass, inverting the shape
Turbid water removes so much light that the pyramid must be perfectly upright
options.misconception: links clarity to pyramid shape without any mechanism

options.text: Pyramid shape depends on temperature gradients, so turbidity is irrelevant
options.misconception: dismisses biomass turnover as a cause of the shape

questions.explanation: In turbid water, small fast-growing producers can support a heavier standing biomass of zooplankton and fish, inverting the biomass pyramid. Clarity alone does not set the shape.
questions.hint: Consider how quickly the base organism reproduces.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate energy dissipated during straw decomposition
questions.stem: A windrow operator has 500,000 kJ of energy in straw and knows decomposers convert 5 percent of that into their own biomass. How many kJ of that energy is dissipated as heat?
questions.explanation: Decomposer biomass holds 5 percent of 500,000 kJ, which is 25,000 kJ, so the remaining 475,000 kJ is spent in respiration and released as heat. Most energy in dead straw leaves the system this way.
questions.hint: Five percent is kept; the rest is lost as heat.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why an omnivore occupies more than one trophic position
questions.stem: An ecologist says the otters of a river, which eat fish, frogs and crayfish, sit at the top of the food web. Why is that only partly true?

options.text: Otters take energy from several levels, so they transfer energy between them rather than sitting at one
Otters are secondary consumers only, since crayfish are the only prey they truly value
options.misconception: ignores fish and frogs in the diet of the otters

options.text: Otters are apex predators, since three prey types make them the top of the web
options.misconception: confuses a varied diet with a single top position

options.text: Otters are indeed at the top, because no animal in the river regularly eats them
options.misconception: confuses being unpredated with being a single fixed level

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish exponential growth from linear growth in a count series
questions.stem: A technician records a bacterial count of 500, 700, 1,000, 1,400 and 1,960 over five hourly readings. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.misconception: treats a constant absolute gain as a capacity ceiling

options.text: The population is declining, since each reading is smaller than the one before it
options.misconception: reads the rising counts as a decline

options.misconception: claims a stable count where the count clearly rises

options.text: The population is growing exponentially, since each gain is about 40 percent of the last count

questions.explanation: Each increase is about 40 percent of the previous count, so the growth is exponential because gains scale with the population. Constant absolute gains would be linear growth instead.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict how a drought changes a population's carrying capacity
questions.stem: An island reserve manager asks how the grazing deer population would react to a long drought that halves the grass.

options.text: The population would hold steady, because deer can survive on shrubs once the grass is gone
options.misconception: ignores the loss of total forage when grass declines

options.text: The population would double, because drought concentrates the remaining animals into a smaller area
options.misconception: confuses crowding with a higher growth rate

options.misconception: ignores deaths in a population accounting

options.text: The population would fall as carrying capacity drops, with deaths exceeding births until numbers match

questions.explanation: A drought lowers the food supply and therefore the carrying capacity. With births below deaths, the herd shrinks until it once again fits the resources that remain.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a reed bed needs producers to support fish
questions.stem: A reed-bed designer wants the bed to support fish without adding fertiliser. Which option best explains the need?

The bed works without producers because detritus alone can feed a whole food web

options.text: Energy is captured by producers and shrinks at each step of this feeding sequence

options.misconception: explains a feeding gradient with temperature tolerance

options.text: The survey is counting species richness rather than numbers, so the values cannot be compared
options.misconception: misreads a density series as a species count

options.text: The gradient shows that trout are strongly territorial and exclude the other two groups
options.misconception: attributes a trophic gradient to territorial exclusion

questions.explanation: Each step from plants to insect larvae to fish passes on only a fraction of the energy, so numbers fall too. The survey shows the expected structure of a feeding sequence, not a temperature effect.
questions.hint: Connect the counts to the energy in each level.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a large producer stock can support few herbivores
questions.stem: A forestry engineer says a mature forest with far more trees than deer still feeds far fewer deer. How?

options.misconception: blames light availability rather than energy transfer

options.misconception: locates the inaccessible energy in the soil instead

options.text: Much of the tree energy goes into wood and leaf tissue that deer cannot digest or reach

questions.explanation: The rule of ten percent limits the energy reaching each consumer level, and much of a tree's energy is locked in wood that deer cannot digest. A large producer crop means little for deer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY

questions.stem: A grass field fixes 20,000 kJ of energy in one season and spends 1,000 kJ of it on its own respiration. How many kJ remain stored in plant biomass?
questions.explanation: Respiration by the grass itself uses 1,000 kJ, so the energy left in standing biomass is 20,000 minus 1,000, which is 19,000 kJ. This is the amount available to herbivores in the field.

questions.stem: A conservation team says protecting a large forest block is the best way to protect a top predator. Why?

options.text: The forest block holds more individual animals than the predator's hunting ground
options.misconception: counts individuals rather than energy

options.text: Forests are warmer than grassland, so the predator prefers the forest for breeding
options.misconception: makes predator presence depend on temperature

options.text: The top predator depends on the energy the producers capture and pass up the pyramid
Protecting the forest stops all the dead material from reaching the predator's scavengers
options.misconception: invents a negative effect of forest protection on scavengers

questions.explanation: A predator occupies the top of an energy pyramid, so it is sustained by energy captured lower down. Protecting the producers that supply that energy protects every level above them.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why decomposers and detritivores are so numerous

options.text: Decomposers and detritivores are numerous because they exploit a wide spread of dead material
Fungi are more efficient at photosynthesis than the trees that grow above them
options.misconception: credits fungi with photosynthesis

options.misconception: claims insects outcompete large browsers for foliage

options.text: The forest floor is too shaded for trees, so fungi took over the whole ecosystem
options.misconception: explains fungi abundance by shading rather than decay

questions.explanation: Dead material is a widespread, reliable resource, so decomposers and detritivores can be very numerous. Fungi are not photosynthetic, and low deer counts reflect predation and energy limits.

options.text: An omnivore, because it takes energy from animals and from human food waste
A carnivore that occasionally overeats, since worms are not a real food source
options.misconception: treats one minor prey item as disqualifying

options.text: A detritivore, because much of its food is waste rather than living prey
options.misconception: confuses refuse with dead organic material

questions.explanation: An omnivore eats both plant material and animals, and here refuse, fish and invertebrates all feature. A dominant food item does not by itself define the feeding category of a species.
questions.hint: Look at the range of food types, not the biggest one.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why adding one resource does not remove other limits
questions.stem: A park designer adds nesting platforms for birds and expects the bird population to rise forever. What limits it?

options.misconception: assumes more nest sites must increase competition

options.text: Carrying capacity still applies, because nest sites are only one of the resources that limit the birds

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity reflects the combined effect of every limiting resource, and nest sites are rarely the only one. Food, predators, disease and territory all still constrain the birds.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise accelerating losses caused by crowding
questions.stem: A farm survey counts chicks at 400, 390, 360 and 300 across four successive weeks of one season. What best explains the decline?

options.text: Density-dependent crowding, since losses accelerate as the birds compete for the same space
A single cold snap in week two, which removed a fixed number of birds each week
options.misconception: attributes a steady decline to one isolated weather event

options.text: Too many predators, since predation is always density independent in crowded systems
options.misconception: calls predation density independent in all circumstances

options.text: No density effect, because the fall in numbers is too regular to reflect crowding
options.misconception: rejects a density effect because the decline looks smooth

questions.explanation: Weekly losses grow larger as the birds crowd together, pointing to density-dependent limits such as competition for space and food. A weather shock would remove a roughly constant number each time.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the missing producer layer in an insect-only roof habitat
questions.stem: A rooftop gardener notices that only flies and aphids live under the sedum roof, and asks what is missing.

options.text: More insects, because the roof already supports two consumer groups and needs a third

options.text: A producer layer, because the insects depend on plants that can capture solar energy
A predator, because the insects must be eaten before the roof can work

options.text: Deeper soil, because the plants will appear once the roots have more room
options.misconception: explains missing producers with soil depth alone

questions.explanation: Every consumer in the roof needs energy that only producers can capture, so a web without plants has no energy source. Adding more insects or a predator adds consumers, not the base.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate energy lost in a single step of a food chain
questions.stem: A food chain carries 20,000 kJ at the producer level, 2,000 kJ at the first consumer level and 200 kJ at the second. How many kJ are lost between the second and third consumer levels?
questions.explanation: At the second consumer level there are 200 kJ, and the third level receives about a tenth of that, which is 20 kJ. The energy lost in that single step is 200 minus 20, or 180 kJ.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reject claims that ignore the transfer efficiency ceiling
questions.stem: A fish farmer argues that a diet of 30 percent protein will let his pond support three times the fish of a 20 percent diet. Why is that wrong?

options.text: Protein percentage is irrelevant, since fish size depends only on the pond volume
options.misconception: dismisses diet quality as a factor in growth

options.text: The rule of ten percent forbids any improvement in feed at all
options.misconception: treats the rule as a ban on better feeding

options.text: Transfer efficiency sets a ceiling, so richer food raises the ceiling only slightly, not threefold
Tripling the fish would also triple the oxygen demand, so the pond would suffocate
options.misconception: makes a valid oxygen point but ignores the ceiling

questions.explanation: The rule of ten percent limits how much ingested energy becomes new tissue, so a better diet narrows the loss but cannot multiply the result. No feed can triple the standing crop of a food web.
questions.hint: Think about the ceiling the rule sets.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the tenfold loss pattern in a measured energy budget
questions.stem: A thermal engineer measures 500 joules of energy entering a beetle population, 50 joules in the mice that eat them and 5 joules in the weasels that eat the mice. What is the pattern?

options.text: A steady tenfold loss at each step, with most energy leaving as heat at every level
A loss of only half at each step, which is far more efficient than expected
options.misconception: mistranslates the figures as a 50 percent transfer

options.text: No pattern, because energy budgets cannot be measured for free-living animals
options.misconception: claims the measurements are impossible to take

options.text: Energy created at each level, because each predator makes more energy than it eats
options.misconception: claims predation generates rather than transfers energy

questions.explanation: Each step keeps about a tenth of the energy, and the rest is used in metabolism and released as heat. This steady tenfold decline is the standard signature of energy flow through a food chain.
questions.hint: Compare each level with the one before it.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about pyramid shape in a community with several producers
questions.stem: A tank designer asks which pyramid correctly represents the energy in a mixed community of plants, algae and bacteria.

options.text: An inverted pyramid, because bacteria are the largest energy store in any mixed community
options.misconception: claims bacteria always dominate the energy base

options.text: An upright pyramid, because producers always hold more energy than the levels above them
A flat pyramid, because mixed communities always balance their energy at each level
options.misconception: assumes mixed communities are always in balance

options.misconception: treats one community as two separate food webs

questions.explanation: However many producers there are, energy still falls at each step, so the energy pyramid narrows upward. A mixed community may hold a flat biomass pyramid and still have an upright energy pyramid.
questions.hint: Mixing producers does not change the transfer rule.

options.misconception: assumes all fish in a lake eat the same thing

The lake chemistry changes when a fish dies, altering how all the species behave

questions.stem: A weed survey records 12, 24, 48 and 96 seedlings across four patches of equal area. What does the sequence indicate?

A stable population, because four equal patches should hold four equal seedling counts

options.misconception: treats any large number as the carrying capacity

options.misconception: invents a keystone role for a growing population

options.text: Not indefinitely, because food, space and disease still set a carrying capacity without predators

options.misconception: credits shading rather than water access
